title: A galaxy model finds a route to rapid star formation at cosmic dawn
freshness: Unreviewed arXiv preprint first submitted October 7, 2026; preliminary and within the preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: A new version of the SAGE galaxy-evolution model can produce massive galaxies early in cosmic history by allowing short periods of very efficient star formation. The result offers one possible explanation for why JWST has found surprisingly massive galaxies at high redshift, while remaining a model-dependent interpretation rather than a direct observation of the mechanism.
whyItMatters: JWST has forced astronomers to revisit how quickly the first large galaxies could assemble. SAGE26 shows that changing how gas reaches galaxies and allowing brief feedback-free starbursts can reproduce several population-level observations without abandoning the broader framework of galaxy evolution.

exploreFurther.label: Read the SAGE26 Paper I preprint

whatToExploreNext: What observations could distinguish feedback-free starbursts from other explanations for unexpectedly massive early galaxies?

sources.label: Bradley et al., SAGE26 Paper I, arXiv preprint

body:
## Why the first big galaxies are difficult to explain

The James Webb Space Telescope has found galaxies in the early universe that appear surprisingly massive for their age. The universe was only a small fraction of its current age when some of these systems were already forming stars rapidly and building substantial stellar populations. That does not automatically break the standard cosmological model, but it does put pressure on the details of how simulations and analytic models turn gas into stars.

A new preprint introduces SAGE26, an updated version of the semi-analytic SAGE model of galaxy evolution. Semi-analytic models do not simulate every parcel of gas directly. Instead, they follow the growth of dark-matter halos and use simplified physical prescriptions for processes such as gas cooling, star formation, stellar feedback and black-hole activity. Their strength is speed: researchers can explore large galaxy populations and test how different physical assumptions affect the statistics we observe.

## A new route for very rapid star formation

SAGE26 adds five observationally motivated changes to the earlier model. One of the most consequential is a feedback-free starburst pathway. In this regime, gas can form stars so efficiently that stellar feedback does not have enough time to regulate the burst before a large fraction of the available gas is converted into stars.

The model also changes how gas reaches galaxies. In lower-mass halos, gas inflow is limited by the time it takes material to fall inward under gravity. In more massive halos, where hot atmospheres can form, the rate is instead controlled by how quickly the gas can cool. These two regimes help the model move gas into galaxies in a way that depends on halo mass and cosmic epoch.

When the authors combine these changes, SAGE26 can produce massive high-redshift galaxies at abundances closer to those inferred from JWST observations. At the same time, the model reproduces broad population-level measurements such as the galaxy stellar mass function and the cosmic star-formation-rate density across much of cosmic time. The team also reports that the model code and data products are open source.

## What the model does not prove

This result is not a direct observation of a feedback-free starburst inside a specific early galaxy. It is a demonstration that such a pathway, together with the other SAGE26 updates, can bring a model into better agreement with several datasets. Different combinations of physical assumptions could potentially reproduce some of the same observations.

That distinction matters because agreement with population statistics does not uniquely identify the mechanism responsible. Galaxy formation models contain linked assumptions about cooling, inflow, star formation, feedback and mergers. Improving one set of predictions can sometimes shift tension elsewhere. The paper is also an unreviewed preprint, so its methods and conclusions have not yet completed peer review.

## Turning JWST surprises into testable physics

The value of SAGE26 is that it converts an observational puzzle into a set of physical hypotheses that can be tested. If rapid, weakly regulated bursts were common at cosmic dawn, future observations should reveal characteristic patterns in stellar ages, gas fractions, dust, metallicity and burst timescales. Those measurements can help separate this explanation from alternatives such as different star-formation efficiencies, revised feedback prescriptions or uncertainties in stellar-mass estimates.

**Measured:** JWST and other surveys provide the galaxy populations that motivate the model comparisons.

**Inferred:** SAGE26 shows that a feedback-free starburst channel and revised gas-inflow physics can reproduce unusually massive early galaxies within a semi-analytic framework, but the mechanism itself remains a model prediction rather than an observed fact.
